current homelab setup for local AI experimentation:

- hermes box hosted on a Framework Desktop Mainboard AI Max+ 395
- 5090 eGPU running Qwen 3.8 27B for fast tok/s LLM use - sometimes 150+ tok/s
- 2x DGX Spark: running Deepseek v4 Flash 0731 - better but slower model
- pi 5 for monitoring
- Mac mini as a dev box - use Herdr and ohmypi/codex/claude depending on the use case
- housed in a 10" DeskPi mini rack (mostly)

Hermes is defaulted to local AI but with a homegrown routing plugin hitting a small low TTFT model (Arch-Router) to decide whether to go local or upgrade to cloud/frontier. Trying to get to 100% local over time, but right now probably more like 60-70%

The Sparks are for batch processing background runs (all the cron jobs, longer dev builds, etc)

do you need all of this? Absolutely not lol. I started with the mac mini and couldn't help myself but to add over time!

Also I regret getting the eGPU so I wouldn't recommend that to anyone

There's a deep duality between the two environments. One of the more interesting things happening in the economy right now is the tug-of-war between housing and AI-related business investment.

Housing has been weak for years, and normally that kind of weakness would be a major recession warning.

But housing is only one part of the economy’s cyclical engine.

Durable goods consumption has been improving, while business equipment investment has accelerated sharply, led by computer equipment tied to the AI capital spending boom.

So while housing is moving in one direction, AI-related investment is moving strongly in the other.

Residential investment, durable goods consumption, and business equipment investment together make up what I call Cyclical GDP. These areas are only about 20% of the economy, but they drive most of the booms and busts.

So far, strength in durable goods and business equipment has been enough to more than offset the weakness in housing.

Housing weakness still matters. But housing by itself has not been enough to push the broader economy into a downturn.

If the Fed starts raising rates again, that will put further pressure on the housing sector. The key issue is not whether housing keeps contracting, but whether housing weakness eventually becomes strong enough to pull down the economy’s cyclical engine.

That would turn today’s tug-of-war into a much broader cyclical problem.

For now, the cyclical economy as a whole is turning higher after a multi-year soft patch.

Hashcats is a fun concept, similar to an idea I've been wanting to put out there for a while.

Problem is that it's inherently an automated ponzi, in the classic sense: new mints pay out older minters.

Mint price increases with each epoch, and floor must necessarily keep up or else you end up in a death spiral:  mint price higher than floor -> people stop minting -> older cats stop getting paid -> they dump -> floor goes lower -> gap widens -> and so on

I like the idea and I think one or two small tweaks could produce a genuinely (long term) engaging ecosystem.

Might have been the push I needed to dust off my old ideabook
